selected.name: Implied Unseen Backstory
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption implies a vivid, hilarious, and logically sound sequence of events that must have preceded the frozen cartoon frame. Score 0 if the caption only addresses the exact moment depicted without suggesting any prior action.
selected.rationale: The dense model heavily favors captions that use the static image as a springboard for an implied narrative. R26 implies a whole history of magic wishes gone wrong, and R32 creates a funny backstory about the bird's career progression.

selected.name: Impact-Per-Word Efficiency
selected.instruction: Score 0 if the caption is long relative to its comedic payoff. Score 10 if the caption delivers a complete, layered joke in very few words (1–6 words), where every word is load-bearing and none are filler.
selected.rationale: R08 (one word) and R20 ('he got indicted' — three words) both achieve maximal compression. R48 ('it's so ewe' — three words) similarly. The dense model rewards the efficiency; the scorecard may prefer more elaborated jokes.

selected.name: Multi-Element Integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when two or more separate visual details interact to produce one unified comic meaning; score 0 when the caption uses only one broad premise or lists details without connecting them.
selected.rationale: R16 links the Earth piñata, the angels’ boss, and the six-day creation story. R39 links the piano’s 88 keys with the damaged house’s missing locks, while R03 combines the table and performance hazards.

selected.name: Deadpan Tone Contrast
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the caption's delivery is completely emotionless, dry, and understated, creating a sharp contrast with the visual's extreme chaos or absurdity. Score 0 if the caption is highly emotional, exclamatory, or acknowledges the absurdity directly.
selected.rationale: The dense model values the comedic clash between extreme visual absurdity and a perfectly deadpan reaction. R01 treats a likely disaster with dry acceptance, and R24 delivers a historic pun with deadpan Holmesian understatement.

selected.name: Surprise reinterpretation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the ending forces a sharp, understandable second reading of the setup; score 0 when the punchline is predictable description without a turn.
selected.rationale: R41 pivots from an ordinary restaurant shutdown to a historical threat, and R54 transforms a family scene into the aftermath of a magical wish.

selected.name: Exact pun construction
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a sound, spelling, name, or word substitution is precise, recognizable, and tightly image-linked; score 0 when the pun is forced, vague, or absent.
selected.rationale: R09, R39, and R46 demonstrate compact, exact wordplay tied to the piano, sheep, and crossword scenes.

selected.name: Controlled boundary-pushing
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an edgy, dark, or suggestive implication is clearly anchored to the cartoon and used for a purposeful punchline; score 0 when shock value is gratuitous, confusing, or offensive without comic structure.
selected.rationale: R03 uses sexual ambiguity within the oversized-meat scene, while R45 turns consent language toward the mosquito’s exposed-skin behavior.

selected.name: Familiar-phrase transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable idiom, lyric, title, or saying is altered so its new wording precisely fits the image; score 0 when the phrase is used unchanged or the reference is arbitrary.
selected.rationale: R18 transforms the phrase about a cross word to fit a crossword, while R47 adapts pulling wool over someone’s eyes to the wolf’s disguise.

selected.name: In-world causal explanation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption supplies a coherent reason for the absurd situation; score 0 when it is unrelated or contradicts the depicted world.
selected.rationale: R08 explains the enormous meat through an imagined consequence, and R49 turns the kitchen traps into a coherent family backstory.

selected.name: Caption-Image Inseparability
selected.instruction: Score 0 if the caption's humor would survive essentially unchanged if paired with many different cartoons. Score 10 if the caption's humor is wholly dependent on this specific image; neither caption alone nor image alone produces the joke.
selected.rationale: R25 ('now the house has 88 keys and no locks') is meaningless without a piano-crashed house; R17 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') only detonates against a wolf in a sheep costume. Contrast with R53 ('when I was a kid, we had to catch our own fish'), a generic 'back in my day' joke that could accompany many bear/cartoon scenarios.

selected.name: Central-anomaly targeting
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption hinges on the cartoon’s most visually peculiar feature; score 0 when it could fit almost any scene.
selected.rationale: The kitchen’s extreme security drives R07, and the living-room circus drives R19; both demonstrate value from targeting the central visual anomaly.

selected.name: Dual-Code Wordplay Activation
selected.instruction: Score 0 if no word or phrase carries simultaneous literal-visual and figurative-idiomatic meanings. Score 10 if a key word/phrase is literally anchored in a visible element AND figuratively creates an additional comic layer, where removing either reading collapses the joke.
selected.rationale: R22 ('you need to get your act together' — circus act + get organized) and R29 ('gravity of our situation' — physical height + seriousness) both hinge on words that are simultaneously literal to the image and figuratively idiomatic, which the dense model credits and the scorecard likely misses. R26 ('bring a lot to the table') is another prime example.

selected.name: Conversational Speech-Act Fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds like a natural utterance from someone situated in the depicted interaction and responds to the exact moment; score 0 when it reads like a detached slogan, label, or headline.
selected.rationale: R04 sounds like a practical reply between people facing the trapped kitchen, R44 sounds like an intimate correction, and R51 uses a recognizable conversational pivot.

selected.name: Character voice fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the implied speaker’s knowledge, attitude, and vocabulary strongly fit the depicted character; score 0 when any character could say it without adjustment.
selected.rationale: R05 and R55 use a bear’s relationship to catching fish, while R30 supplies a comparatively interchangeable human remark.

selected.name: Functional cultural allusion
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable cultural or institutional reference directly transforms the cartoon’s specific details; score 0 when the reference is obscure, decorative, or detachable from the image.
selected.rationale: R51 and R56 turn costume-shopping and a living-room parade into specific public-world references rather than adding unrelated name-dropping.

selected.name: Direct pun or wordplay reliance
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the caption's humor relies entirely on a literal pun, homophone, or direct wordplay matching an element in the drawing. 0 = no wordplay, 10 = the entire joke is a simple pun. Do not judge whether puns are good or bad.
selected.rationale: Heavy reliance on direct wordplay is a common textual fingerprint of high 'joke density' that scores well on generic checklists but often lacks the narrative depth required by the contest. See R04 (wreckmaninoff) and R29 (ewe).

selected.name: Cultural-name familiarity load
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much understanding the caption depends on a named person, brand, institution, title, or other proper cultural reference; do not judge whether the allusion is good.
selected.rationale: Audience familiarity with external names can influence reception independently of the line's fit to the drawing. Examples include Gibson in R25, Rachmaninoff in R45, and the White House in R52.

selected.name: List-normalization typography
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text shows raw-entry or transcription conventions such as lowercase starts, omitted terminal punctuation, doubled hyphens, repeated punctuation, or dialect apostrophes; do not judge whether the typography improves the caption.
selected.rationale: Compilation or submission conventions leave visible formatting traces that can be predictive while being unrelated to the cartoon joke. Examples include lowercase, unpunctuated R01 and R08, and the dialect or dash usage in R24 and R30.

selected.name: Era-coded idiom
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses period-marked slang, archaic wording, song or title allusions, or culturally dated phrasing; do not judge whether the wording is amusing or appropriate.
selected.rationale: An entry’s era in the contest series can leave lexical fingerprints even when the cartoon-specific idea is unchanged. Such dating is nuisance information rather than intrinsic fit, visible in ‘two-step program’ in R17, ‘comin’ round the mountain’ in R24, and ‘old cowhand’ in R37.

selected.name: Generic caption closure
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the line has a generic, self-contained setup-to-punch structure with an obvious semantic mapping that a general-purpose writer could readily produce; do not judge whether the joke is good.
selected.rationale: Well-formed, immediately legible caption shapes are easy for a generic prior to nominate even when editorial taste differs. R22, R37, and R56 all use straightforward premise-to-punch constructions.

selected.name: News-cycle topicality
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption invokes identifiable contemporary political, public-event, or news-cycle language; do not judge whether the caption is good.
selected.rationale: Live political framing can attract text-model attention independently of cartoon-specific merit. Examples include the Republican references in R05, R32, and R36, and the voting reference in R09.

selected.name: Norm-challenging register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the caption uses sexual, consent-related, bodily, violent, or otherwise socially provocative language; do not judge whether the language is good or appropriate.
selected.rationale: Provocative wording can draw attention or trigger audience reactions unrelated to cartoon-specific merit. The sexual reference in R30 and consent language in R40 are clear examples; bodily harm also appears in R54.

selected.name: Format-native compression
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the caption use a compressed, standalone one-liner that omits setup and relies on the reader to supply the visual context? Score only this structural feature; do not judge whether the compression is good or apt.
selected.rationale: A serial entrant's practiced economy may leave terse, context-dependent lines, while practice may also sometimes improve actual writing. R01 and R33 are highly compressed, visually dependent one-liners.

selected.name: Stock setup wording
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses reusable conversational scaffolding such as ‘I think,’ ‘remember when,’ ‘I don’t know,’ ‘you should,’ or ‘let me’; do not judge whether the resulting joke is good.
selected.rationale: A serial entrant may internalize recurring caption openings, creating a textual practice fingerprint. Such discipline may also genuinely help timing, so this is mixed; the pattern appears in R09, R23, R52, and R54.

selected.name: Magazine-safe restraint
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the caption uses a clean, non-explicit, socially restrained register, avoiding profanity, graphic sexuality or violence, and overtly abrasive language; do not judge whether restraint is desirable.
selected.rationale: A publication’s house style can produce a stable register fingerprint independent of the particular image. That register may also contribute to actual suitability, so this is mixed; restrained examples include R04, R12, R19, and R57.

b_merge.judge_roster_deviation: Rounds 1-4 used sealed Claude subagents (Sonnet + Opus) as the two blind merge judges. This session's Claude subagent budget was exhausted after round 4, so round 5's two judges are gpt-5.6-luna and glm-5.2 -- still two independent frontier models in two different families, still blind, still STRICT (both must say SAME), both planted identity anchors passed for both. The models' SELF-REPORTED names in their JSON ('GPT-5', 'gpt-4o') are wrong and are not the endpoints that were called; the authoritative identities are in each verdict file's _judge_meta block.
